Conduct population-based drug-resistance surveillance to assess the impact of long-term isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) programs on drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) within the community. This includes monitoring changes in mono-isoniazid resistance, mono-rifampicin resistance, and multidrug-resistant TB. 2. 3. Studies conducted in South Africa, Botswana, and India have evaluated the efficacy of different TB preventive regimens in HIV-infected individuals. For example, the Swaminathan et al. (2012) study compared a six-month isoniazid plus ethambutol regimen to other approaches, while the Martinson et al. (2011) study assessed continuous and six-month isoniazid regimens over a median follow-up of 47 months. 4. The Samandari et al. (2011) study, which likely had a median follow-up of 36 months, did not clearly describe allocation concealment, potentially introducing selection bias. Similarly, the Swaminathan et al. (2012) and Martinson et al. (2011) studies were not blinded, which could have influenced outcomes. 5. Differences in patient populations were noted across studies. For instance, the Martinson et al. (2011) study excluded patients eligible for antiretroviral therapy (ART) and had a median baseline CD4 count of 484 cells/mm³. In contrast, the Samandari et al. (2011) study included 2% of participants on ART at enrollment, with 47% on ART by month 36, and a median baseline CD4 count of 297 cells/mm³. The Swaminathan et al. (2012) study included ART-naïve patients with a median baseline CD4 count of 325 cells/mm³. 6. The control group in the Swaminathan et al. (2012) study received 300 mg of isoniazid and 800 mg of ethambutol. The Martinson et al. (2011) study included only patients with a positive tuberculin skin test (TST) result (>5 mm). 7. Although allocation concealment in the Samandari et al. (2011) study was not clearly described, this was not deemed sufficient to downgrade the study for risk of bias. 8. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends providing 36 months of isoniazid preventive therapy to adults and adolescents living with HIV in resource-constrained settings with high TB and HIV prevalence. 9. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) system is used to assess the certainty of evidence. High-certainty evidence indicates a very low likelihood of substantial differences in the effect, while moderate-certainty evidence suggests a moderate likelihood. Low-certainty evidence indicates a high likelihood of substantial differences, and very low-certainty evidence provides unreliable indications of the effect. 10. The GRADE Working Group, established in 2000, developed a transparent and standardized approach to grading the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. This approach has been adopted by many international organizations to improve decision-making in healthcare. 11. References include studies by Martinson et al. (2011), Samandari et al. (2011), Swaminathan et al. (2012), and others, which provide insights into the cost-effectiveness and efficacy of TB preventive therapy in HIV-infected populations across various settings.
